intro: TRACE is a small, runnable slice of a larger idea: take requirements to reviewed, traceable test cases with AI-style agents and a human in the loop, then keep going all the way to executed, reported results. This page is what already works and what I am considering next.

items.title: Requirements to reviewed test cases
items.summary: Projects, cycles and requirements; five specialised agents (functional, API, security, performance, integration) run in parallel and stream each test case live.
items.why: Specialised agents give broader, higher quality coverage than one big prompt, and streaming makes long runs feel observable instead of stuck.

items.title: Human review gate with server-side roles
items.summary: Approve, reject or bulk-review cases. Roles (viewer, tester, qa lead, admin) are enforced by the API, not only hidden in the UI.
items.why: An AI output should never reach a downstream step unchecked, and a button that is only disabled in the browser is not a gate.

items.title: Requirement to test case traceability matrix
items.summary: Every case links to the requirement version it was written against; the matrix shows covered, pending review and uncovered requirements.
items.why: Coverage claims need evidence you can show to an auditor or a release manager.

items.title: Requirement versioning, stale detection and incremental regeneration
items.summary: Editing a requirement bumps its version and flags linked cases as stale. Incremental mode regenerates only what changed and leaves every other approval alone.
items.why: Specs change constantly. Regenerating everything throws away reviewed work and trains people to stop reviewing.

items.title: Choose the generator: built-in rules, Claude or ChatGPT
items.summary: Use the offline rule engine, or paste your own Claude (Anthropic) or ChatGPT (OpenAI) API key to have a model write the cases. Output is validated before it is stored, and the key is never saved.
items.why: Anyone can compare a model against deterministic rules on the same requirements, with nothing to install and no data leaving the machine unless they choose it.

items.title: Grounding checks on model output
items.summary: Every model-written case must quote the requirement sentence it verifies. Cases with no quote, a quote that is not there, or invented endpoints and fields are dropped or flagged. The model can ask clarification questions instead of guessing.
items.why: A fluent test case about behaviour nobody specified is worse than no test case, because it looks reviewed.

items.title: Project knowledge and learning from review
items.summary: Per-project terms, rules and avoid notes go into every model run. Corrected and approved cases become examples; rejected cases with a note become warnings.
items.why: The fastest way to fix a repeated mistake is to tell the generator once, in the project, not in every prompt.

items.title: Golden-set evaluation
items.summary: scripts/run_eval.py scores any generator for criteria coverage, must-cover phrases and invented content, and fails when thresholds are missed. CI runs it.
items.why: Without a measurement, a prompt change is a guess.

items.title: Ready for a team: Docker, admin users, CSV import
items.summary: Dockerfile and compose file, first admin from environment, a Team tab for users and roles, CSV requirement import with per-line errors, automatic column upgrades, and a startup check against the placeholder signing key.
items.why: A tool others cannot install, sign in to and load data into does not get used.

items.title: Cross-cycle coverage baseline
items.summary: Compare a new cycle against previously approved cases so gap detection says 'this requirement was covered last release, now it is not'.
items.why: Today gaps only look inside one cycle. A baseline is what turns gap detection from a list into a regression signal.

items.title: End-to-end journey agent as its own type
items.summary: A dedicated agent for multi-screen journeys, one case per journey, with the UI only offering types that really produce output.
items.why: Offering an option that silently produces nothing is worse than not offering it.

items.title: Locator-verified script generation from approved cases
items.summary: Turn approved cases into Playwright page-object scripts, then check every generated locator against the live app before the script is stored.
items.why: Checking before storing is cheaper than repairing after a run fails, and it removes most flaky-locator failures up front.

items.title: Script review gate and Git check-in on a branch
items.summary: Approved scripts go through a second human gate, then land on a per-cycle branch with a pull request. The API refuses check-in unless the gate is approved.
items.why: Generated code deserves the same review path as written code.

items.title: Dry run in a disposable workspace
items.summary: Run generated scripts in an isolated per-run workspace, capture before/after evidence, and produce a single self-contained HTML report that still opens offline.
items.why: A proving ground between 'generated' and 'trusted', without touching shared systems.

items.title: Execution with a browser matrix and schedules
items.summary: Run approved suites across browsers, resume after a closed tab, and schedule runs that skip a tick instead of stacking up when one is already active.
items.why: Runs belong on the server, not in a tab. Wait-on-active scheduling avoids pile-ups.

items.title: Insights, trends and one-click bug creation
items.summary: Rule-based recommendations (deterministic, no model cost on page load), an executive rollup, a per-run detail view, and raising a bug from a failed result.
items.why: Same input should always give the same advice. A narrative layer from a model can sit on top later.

items.title: Reverse-engineer requirements from a running app
items.summary: Crawl a live app (with a human-assisted login step) into a knowledge graph, then draft requirements and flag ambiguities for a person to resolve.
items.why: Most real applications have stale or missing specs, so start from what the app really does.

items.title: Push to a test management tool with per-user credentials
items.summary: Create or update work items in a test management tool using each user's own token, held server-side and never sent to the browser.
items.why: Actions should be attributable to the person who took them.

items.title: Run load tests and judge them against targets
items.summary: Execute the generated performance scenarios and mark each non-functional target met or breached.
items.why: Generating performance cases is only half the job; the verdict is what people need.

items.title: Multi-worker deployment
items.summary: Swap the in-process event bus for Redis pub/sub and move artifacts from local disk to object storage.
items.why: Evidence stored on one machine's disk ties a run to that machine and blocks horizontal scaling.

items.title: PDF and Excel exports
items.summary: Exports for reports and the traceability matrix, next to the CSV that already works.
items.why: Stakeholders want a file they can attach to an email.

items.title: Self-healing for broken scripts
items.summary: When an executed script fails, classify the failure, inspect the live page and propose a patch that a person accepts, all inside a strict token, time and tool-call budget.
items.why: Worth building only for failures that cannot be prevented by verifying locators when the script is generated.

principles: Checking before you ship is cheaper than repairing after it breaks.
Do not offer a feature in the UI until it is wired up.
A permission that is not enforced on the API route is not a permission.
Keep an audit trail: which input version produced which output, and who approved it.
Prefer deterministic rules; use a model for what rules cannot do.
Regenerate narrowly. Throwing away reviewed work is how a review process dies.
